note: Ten valid segments, one per visual type, taken from the prototype. Use as renderer fixtures and generator few-shot examples.

segments.heading: Read the label from the top
segments.key_idea: Every number on the label is for one serving.
segments.body: Before calories, sugar or protein, find the serving size at the top of the panel. Everything beneath it describes that one amount, so if you eat more, every number grows with it.

visual.title: Start Here
visual.caption: The serving size dictates all other values.

segments.heading: One bag, three servings
segments.key_idea: Multiply by the servings you actually eat.
segments.body: The label lists calories for one serving. This bag holds three, so finishing it means three times the calories, sugar and sodium shown.

segments.heading: Your 60-second label scan
segments.key_idea: Same five checks, same order, every time.
segments.body: Serving size, calories, added sugars and sodium, the 5/20 rule, then the ingredient list. Run them in that order and any label takes about a minute.

segments.heading: Where % Daily Value comes from
segments.key_idea: Every %DV is measured against a 2,000-calorie day.
segments.body: The percentages on the label assume a 2,000-calorie diet. Your own needs may be higher or lower, so treat %DV as a yardstick for comparing foods, not a personal target.

visual.caption: the reference intake behind every % Daily Value

source.name: U.S. FDA
source.title: How to Understand and Use the Nutrition Facts Label

segments.heading: From accepted offer to keys
segments.key_idea: Each stage has to clear before the next can start.
segments.body: Once your offer is accepted, the lender verifies your finances and the property. Underwriting usually takes two to six weeks; after the appraisal and final approval, you sign and get the keys.

segments.heading: Read the back, not the front
segments.key_idea: Ingredients are listed by weight, heaviest first.
segments.body: The front of the pack is there to sell. The ingredient list tells you what is actually inside, and sugar can appear under several different names.

visual.title: Reading the ingredient list
do: Look for hidden sugar names (dextrose, cane syrup)
Compare per 100 g when sizes differ
dont: Judge by the front of the pack

segments.heading: Anatomy of the label
segments.key_idea: Four parts do most of the work.
segments.body: The serving size sets the amount, calories show the energy in it, added sugars flag what was put in during processing, and the % Daily Value column tells you whether each amount is a little or a lot.

segments.heading: What %DV actually means
segments.key_idea: It is a share of a whole day, per serving.
segments.body: The % Daily Value turns grams and milligrams into a percentage you can compare at a glance. It is based on a 2,000-calorie diet, so it is a reference point, not a personal prescription.

visual.definition: How much of a day’s recommended amount one serving gives you, based on a 2,000-calorie diet.
visual.example: 20% DV of sodium = one fifth of your day’s salt in one serving.

segments.heading: Low, high, or in between
segments.key_idea: 5% DV or less is low. 20% DV or more is high.
segments.body: Use the 5/20 rule on any nutrient with a %DV. At 12%, this cereal’s sodium sits between the two: worth noticing, especially if you have more than one serving.

segments.heading: Spot a dual-column label
segments.key_idea: One column per serving, one for the whole package.
segments.body: Some packages that could be eaten in one sitting or several show two columns: one for a single serving and one for the entire package, so you don’t have to do the math.
